An oyster is a little jar of the sea it grew in. Every one on this platter tastes of different water.
For centuries, oysters were food for the poor. In New York, six cents bought all you could eat.
Then sewage closed the beds. The last one in New York shut in nineteen twenty-seven. Now a single oyster costs over three dollars.
So why a dollar at five o'clock? The bar pays about seventy-seven cents for each one. After the shucker is paid, it loses money.
That's the trick. The cheap oyster fills the seats, and the drinks pay for it.
The taste comes from survival. An oyster matches the salt around it by filling its cells with amino acids, mostly taurine. Saltier water, more savoury oyster.
So place matters. Cold northern bays give briny oysters. The warm Gulf gives mild ones. The Pacific coast tastes of cucumber and melon.
Season matters too. Oysters are plumpest before they spawn in summer. Then they turn milky, and warm water brings Vibrio bacteria.
The priciest aren't a different animal, just older, rarer or bigger. A Coffin Bay King grows six years and sold for a hundred Australian dollars.
And a good one? Shut tight, heavy, full of liquor, smelling of the sea. Ask to see the tag.
